description_full: Griffon Corporation, through its subsidiaries, provides home and building, and consumer and professional products in the United States, Canada, Australia, and internationally. The Building Products segment manufactures and markets residential and sectional commercial garage doors, rolling steel service doors, fire doors, shutters, steel security grilles, and room dividers. It also provides residential, industrial, and commercial ceiling fans under Hunter, Casablanca, and Jan Fan brands. The company also sells garage door openers. In addition, this segment provides home organization products and lawn and garden products. It serves home centers, warehouse clubs, discount stores, commercial distributors, and e-commerce companies. The company was formerly known as Instrument Systems Corporation and changed its name to Griffon Corporation in January 1995. Griffon Corporation was incorporated in 1959 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

financial_summary: Griffon Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $4.9B market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -12% over the past three years and -1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 27%.

The business throws off $267M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.95× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.9×.

Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 18% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Revenue growth in the bottom decile of Industrials peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Trading near 52-week highs — the market has already recognised the story
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $21.8M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 14% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
14 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 23% operating margin runs 14pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.03x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+9.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 35% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 1% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 1.03, it moves roughly with the market.
About $31.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 57% in the 2020 crash, 37% in the 2022 bear market and 52% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 11% below its DCF fair value of $122, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 82%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $48.34 to $300 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 46% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $125 on average, 16% above the price.
The price implies 5.3% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.13).
It runs a 27% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 105% is amplified by 5.6x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 15pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.1x net debt to EBITDA ($98.6M of cash against $1.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.9x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.8, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -11.7% over 3 years, -4.0% over 5 years and -0.6% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 50.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 16% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 7%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 2.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders own 18.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 82%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (38 sales, net $21.8M sold).
It returns 3.9% a year to shareholders (3.1% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 4.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, raising it 18.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 3,355 employees, each generates about $551K of revenue, 1.5x the Industrials median.
That works out to $80K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $9.5M (17x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
